claims.text: The initial catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element metallic alloy containing Cu, Ni, and trace Pt with a uniform matrix.
Controlled surface deposition, such as atomic layer deposition, can create isolated single-atom Pt sites on this alloy.
Co-deposited oxyphilic or nitrogen-donating species can anchor Pt and maintain its atomic dispersion during long-term automotive operation.
Atomic dispersion permits control of the local chemical and electronic environment and can enhance catalytic performance.
Atomically dispersed Pt on the multi-metallic matrix will downshift the Pt d-band center.
The electronic modification of Pt will lower oxidation activation barriers for CO and hydrocarbons.
The altered electronic properties will weaken adsorption of H2O and NO and thereby reduce poisoning.
Strong anchoring of isolated Pt atoms will prevent their sintering and agglomeration during automotive exhaust aging.
The intervention will reduce CO and hydrocarbon oxidation ignition temperatures to below 150 °C relative to the unmodified catalyst.
The intervention will improve resistance to deactivation by H2O and NO relative to the unmodified catalyst.
The intervention will sustain catalytic performance over extended aging and thermal cycling better than the unmodified catalyst.
The unmodified near-equiatomic catalyst has higher ignition temperatures, greater H2O/NO susceptibility, and faster deactivation than the proposed Pt-modified catalyst.
The anticipated improvements depend on retaining truly atomic Pt dispersion, and Pt agglomeration may compromise performance.
The proposed benefit should apply during transient operation below 150 °C, H2O and NO exposure, and accelerated thermal and chemical aging.
Prior literature supports enhanced activity and stability for single-atom Pt catalysts.
Long-term stability of single-atom Pt in a multi-principal-element matrix under real automotive exhaust remains unproven.
The hypothesis is to be tested against an unmodified catalyst using T10 and T50, conversion, deactivation rate, and pre/post-aging Pt dispersion measurements.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant 10–15% ignition-temperature reduction and lower deactivation, or observation of significant Pt agglomeration, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
